sentences.text: Adult Saurosuchus measured between 5.5 and 7 meters in length and weighed up to 590 kilograms.
Sub-adult specimens of Saurosuchus are estimated to have been 4.07 meters long and weighed about 385 kg.
The skull of Saurosuchus could reach 58.6 cm in length, and the largest known skulls measure approximately this size.
The skull was 17 cm wide at the back and narrowed to 10 cm in front of the eyes, featuring a deep structure that was compressed laterally.
Its teeth were large, recurved, and serrated.
Saurosuchus likely had nine shortened and robust cervical vertebrae, creating a strong neck.
The pelvic girdle featured an ischium split into two expansions, with the anterior portion being thinner than the posterior one.
Saurosuchus had two rows of leaf-shaped osteoderms running along the midline of its spine.
Adult Saurosuchus measured between 5.5 and 7 meters in length and weighed up to 590 kilograms.
Saurosuchus was likely the largest member of its group, measuring about 7 meters in length, with the possible exception of the less known Fasolasuchus.
A 2023 analysis estimated Saurosuchus had a surprisingly weak bite for its size, with forces of 1015 and 1885 N at the front and back of the jaws, comparable to modern gharials.
The first Saurosuchus specimen was discovered in 1957 by Galileo J. Scaglia and Leocadio Soria in northwestern Argentina.
The species Saurosuchus galilei was formally named in 1959 by Osvaldo A. Reig, who also named the type species S. galilei.
The name Saurosuchus comes from Greek words meaning 'lizard' and 'crocodile', and the species name 'galilei' honors Galileo J. Scaglia, who discovered and prepared the holotype specimen.
Saurosuchus was likely the apex predator of its Late Triassic environment.
Researchers argue Saurosuchus did not eat bone but instead defleshed carcasses by using its rear teeth to bite off or scrape muscle while avoiding bone contact.
Evidence suggests Saurosuchus relied on smell rather than eyesight to track prey and was not a particularly agile predator.
Analysis of the braincase suggests Saurosuchus had a high hearing range tuned to low frequencies and relied heavily on its sense of smell to find food.
Like other rauisuchians, Saurosuchus walked on four fully extended legs.
A hypertrophied hypophysis in Saurosuchus may be correlated with its large size and rapid growth rates.
Saurosuchus is now classified as a basal member of the clade Loricata, which includes rauisuchians and crocodylomorphs.
Recent analyses place Saurosuchus within the loricatan clade Prestosuchidae.
Saurosuchus lived during the Late Triassic period, specifically from the Late Carnian to the Early Norian stages.

Saurosuchus lived in the Late Triassic in territories of modern-day Argentina, in an environment dominated by fluvial and floodplain areas with strongly seasonal rainfall. Volcanic ash layers in the formation indicate Saurosuchus lived between approximately 231.4 and 227 million years ago, during the Carnian age, from 233.6 to 227.3 million years ago.

It is debated whether Saurosuchus fossils found in the Chinle Formation of Arizona belong to this species or to an indeterminate rauisuchian, as later studies consider isolated teeth and small cranial fragments found there to be from an indeterminate rauisuchian species.
